# Ecclesiastes Chapter 10 -- The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.

**2** A wise man's heart inclines to the right, but a fool's heart to the left.

**3** Even when the fool walks along the road, he lacks sense, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.

**4** If the anger of a ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.

**5** There is an evil I have seen under the sun, the sort of error that arises from a ruler:

**6** Folly is set in many high places, and the rich sit in lowly positions. **7** I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking on foot like servants.

**8** He who digs a pit may fall into it, and a serpent may bite him who breaks through a wall.

**9** He who quarries stones may be hurt by them, and he who splits logs may be endangered by them.

**10** If the iron is blunt and one does not sharpen the edge, he must use more strength, but wisdom brings success.

**11** If the serpent bites before it is charmed, there is no advantage in a charmer.

**12** The words of a wise man's mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him. **13** The beginning of his words is foolishness, and the end of his talk is wicked madness.

**14** A fool multiplies words, though no one knows what is to come, and who can tell him what will happen after him?

**15** The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not even know the way to town.

**16** Woe to you, O land, when your king is a youth, and your princes feast in the morning!

**17** Blessed are you, O land, when your king is of noble birth, and your princes feast at the proper time — for strength and not for drunkenness!

**18** Through laziness the rafters sag; through idle hands the house leaks.

**19** A feast is made for laughter, wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.

**20** Do not curse the king, even in your thoughts, nor curse the rich in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report what you say.

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 10 is Ecclesiastes' most proverbial chapter — a collection of wisdom sayings about fools and wise men, rulers and servants, labor and laziness. The chapter moves from the metaphor of dead flies in perfume (v.1) through observations about social inversion (vv.5–7), practical wisdom about work (vv.8–11), the fool's self-destructive speech (vv.12–15), governance (vv.16–19), and the danger of unguarded speech (v.20). Unlike the philosophical chapters, this material is closer to Proverbs in style — but Qoheleth's characteristic irony pervades it.

---

## Disagreement Log

## 10:1 — "outweighs" vs. "is weightier than"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "weightier than-wisdom and-than-honor [is] a-little folly" | Literal word order |
| LOGOS | "a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor" | Natural English |
| PNEUMA | "a little foolishness outweighs wisdom and honor" | Same sense, "foolishness" instead of "folly" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS wording with "folly" — more concise than "foolishness."

---

## 10:19 — Ironic or literal?

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "money answers everything" | Literal |
| LOGOS | "money answers everything" | Same, preserves ambiguity |
| PNEUMA | "money is the answer for everything" | Slightly more emphatic/ironic |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** All three essentially agree. Adopted "money answers everything" — preserving the Hebrew's terse ambiguity.

---
*-- SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
